Code-based [3,1][3,1]-avoiders in finite affine spaces AG⁡(n,2)\mathrm{AG}(n,2)

Benedek Kovács ††thanks: ELTE Linear Hypergraphs Research Group, Eötvös Loránd University, Budapest, Hungary. The author is supported by the EKÖP-24 University Excellence Scholarship Program of the Ministry for Culture and Innovation from the source of the National Research, Development and Innovation Fund. E-mail: benoke981@gmail.com
\dateformatoneAugust 24, 2026
Abstract

The author, together with Nagy, studied the following problem on unavoidable intersections of given size in binary affine spaces. Given an mm-element set S⊆𝔽2nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, is there guaranteed to be a [k,t][k,t]-flat, that is, a kk-dimensional affine subspace of 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} containing exactly tt points of SS? Such problems can be viewed as generalizations of the cap set problem over the binary field. They conjectured that for every fixed pair (k,t)(k,t) with k≥1k\geq 1 and 0≤t≤2k0\leq t\leq 2^{k}, the density of values m∈{0,…,2n}m\in\{0,...,2^{n}\} for which a [k,t][k,t]-flat is guaranteed tends to 11.

In this paper, motivated by the study of the smallest open case (k,t)=(3,1)(k,t)=(3,1), we present explicit constructions of sets in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} avoiding [k,1][k,1]-flats for exponentially many sizes. These sets rely on carefully constructed binary linear codes, whose weight enumerators determine the size of the construction.

Keywords: affine space, linear code, unavoidable, weight enumerator

1 Introduction

Consider the points of the nn-dimensional affine space AG⁡(n,2)\mathrm{AG}(n,2) over the binary field 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}, which also correspond to the elements of the vector space 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}.

Let S⊆AG⁡(n,2)S\subseteq\mathrm{AG}(n,2) be a point set of a fixed cardinality mm. We investigate the intersections of SS with the kk-dimensional affine subspaces of 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, referred to as kk-flats. We say that SS induces a [k,t][k,t]-flat if there exists a kk-flat Fk⊆𝔽2nF_{k}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} such that |S∩Fk|=t|S\cap F_{k}|=t. Otherwise we say that SS is a [k,t][k,t]-avoider.

Our question is the following: for what quadruples (n,m,k,t)(n,m;k,t) does it hold that every S⊆𝔽2nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} of size mm induces a [k,t][k,t]-flat? If this is true, we write [n,m]→[k,t][n,m]\to[k,t]. The question was posed by the author and Nagy [10] as a qq-analogue of a graph-theoretical problem by Erdős, Füredi, Rothschild and T. Sós [4]. Note that a [k,0][k,0]-avoider is also called a blocking set with respect to kk-dimensional subspaces, which is an extensively covered topic in the projective and affine settings (see [1] for a survey). Also note that the corresponding question in the ternary field 𝔽3\mathbb{F}_{3} contains the well-known cap set problem [3], asking for the largest size of a subset in 𝔽3n\mathbb{F}_{3}^{n} without a full line. This would correspond to k=1k=1 and t=3t=3.

We defined the (n,k,t)(n;k,t)-spectrum Sp⁡(n,k,t)\Sp(n,k,t), and its density, ρ⁡(n,k,t)\rho(n;k,t), by

Sp⁡(n,k,t):={0≤m≤2n:[n,m]→[k,t]},ρ⁡(n,k,t):=|Sp⁡(n,k,t)|2n.\begin{split}\Sp(n;k,t)&:=\{0\leq m\leq 2^{n}:[n,m]\to[k,t]\},\\ \rho(n;k,t)&:=\frac{|\Sp(n;k,t)|}{2^{n}}.\end{split}

Here, and throughout this paper, we assume that (n,k,t)(n,k,t) is a triple of integers with n≥1n\geq 1, 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n and 0≤t≤2k0\leq t\leq 2^{k}.

We presented the following main conjecture:

Conjecture 1.1 (Kovács, Nagy [10]).

For every k≥1k\geq 1 and 0≤t≤2k0\leq t\leq 2^{k}, we have

limn→∞ρ⁡(n,k,t)=1.\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(n;k,t)=1.

The conjecture was shown true for t∈{0,2k−1,2k}t\in\{0,2^{k-1},2^{k}\} when k≥3k\geq 3, and for all tt when k∈{1,2}k\in\{1,2\}. The main result used for this (apart from the basic cases) was a result similar to Szemerédi’s Cube Lemma (see [15, Corollary 2.1]), which also follows from a work of Bonin and Qin [2], stating that for m≥52⋅2n⁡(1−12k−1)m\geq\frac{5}{2}\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\right)}, we have [n,m]→[k,2k][n,m]\to[k,2^{k}]. The proof proceeded by picking the value 𝐝∈𝔽2n\mathbf{d}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} that appears the most commonly as a difference of two elements in SS, and applying the statement inductively for the quotient space 𝔽2n/⟨𝐝⟩\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}/\left\langle\mathbf{d}\right\rangle.

We also showed that lim infρ⁡(n,k,t)>0\liminf\rho(n;k,t)>0 when tt is of the form 2a2^{a} or 3⋅2a3\cdot 2^{a} for some integer 1≤a≤k−21\leq a\leq k-2. The proof of the latter result was more involved, using the notion of additive energy defined by Tao and Vu [17], and bounding sizes of hypercube cuts based on a theorem of Hart [7]. However, 1.1 stays open in these cases too.

Improving on an argument by Guruswami [5], we also used the probabilistic method to obtain so-called [k,c][k,c]-evasive sets, defined as sets in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} intersecting every kk-flat in at most cc points. Our result was the following:

Theorem 1.2.

Let k,c∈ℤ>0k,c\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} with c≥k+1c\geq k+1. Then for some K>0K>0, there exists a [k,c][k,c]-evasive set in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} of size at least K⋅2n⁡(1−kc)K\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{k}{c}\right)} when nn is sufficiently large.

As [k,c][k,c]-evasive sets are [k,t][k,t]-avoiders for every t>ct>c, this theorem can easily be used to show that the number of sizes mm outside Sp⁡(n,k,t)\Sp(n;k,t) is exponentially large for each pair (k,t)(k,t) with k≥3k\geq 3 and (k,t)≠(3,4)(k,t)\neq(3,4). For example, since the complement of any [3,6][3,6]-evasive set is a [3,1][3,1]-avoider, there exist [3,1][3,1]-avoiders of all sizes 2n−K⋅2n/2≤m≤2n2^{n}-K\cdot 2^{n/2}\leq m\leq 2^{n} by Theorem 1.2. However, as these [k,t][k,t]-avoiders are obtained with a random method, there is no systematic way to describe them.

The research presented in this paper mainly concerns the smallest open case of 1.1, which is (k,t)=(3,1)(k,t)=(3,1). Our main result is a construction of an explicit family of [3,1][3,1]-avoiders that still exhibit exponentially many different sizes. We call this the code-based construction, which takes an arbitrary binary linear code as an input, and derives a [k,1][k,1]-avoider (for fixed k≥3k\geq 3) whose size only depends on the weight enumerator of the code evaluated at certain inputs.

Let us make note of the following definitions.

Definition 1.3 (Weight of a codeword).

In a binary linear code CC, the weight of a codeword 𝐱∈C\mathbf{x}\in C is the number of coordinates of 𝐱\mathbf{x} equal to 11.

Definition 1.4 (Weight enumerator).

The weight enumerator of a binary code C⊆𝔽2ℓC\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell} is a bivariate polynomial WCW_{C} defined by

WC​(x,y)=∑w=0ℓAw​xw​yℓ−w,W_{C}(x,y)=\sum_{w=0}^{\ell}A_{w}x^{w}y^{\ell-w},

where ℓ\ell is the length of CC, and AwA_{w} is the number of codewords in CC having weight ww for each 0≤w≤ℓ0\leq w\leq\ell.

For further details on the coding-theoretical terminology used in the paper, see Subsection 2.1. We now state our main results.

Theorem 1.5.

Fix integers k≥3k\geq 3 and ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. Take a binary linear code C≤𝔽2ℓC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell}. Then for n=ℓ⁡(k−1)n=\ell(k-1), there exists a [k,1][k,1]-avoider SS in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} for which |S|=2n−WC​(1,2k−1−1)|S|=2^{n}-W_{C}(1,2^{k-1}-1).

Here the set SS is obtained using the code-based construction, which is detailed in Construction 4.1.

Theorem 1.6.

Suppose that n≥4n\geq 4 is an even integer. Then the number of different sizes of [3,1][3,1]-avoiders in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} given by the code-based construction is at least (⌊(n−4)/4⌋⌊(n−4)/8⌋)1/3≥c⋅2n/12n\binom{\left\lfloor(n-4)/4\right\rfloor}{\left\lfloor(n-4)/8\right\rfloor}^{1/3}\geq c\cdot\frac{2^{n/12}}{\sqrt{n}} for some absolute constant c>0c>0.

Note that here we got at least ≈cn⋅1.059n\approx\frac{c}{\sqrt{n}}\cdot 1.059^{n} different sizes, but as we will remark later, by the MacWilliams identity, the number of different sizes obtainable by this method is bounded above by c⋅n⋅(3)n≈c⋅n⋅1.732nc\cdot n\cdot(\sqrt{3})^{n}\approx c\cdot n\cdot 1.732^{n}.

The outline of the paper is the following. In Section 2, we set the basic notation and definitions. In Section 3, we give examples of [k,1][k,1]-avoiders that are built from affine subspaces using union and symmetric difference operations. We then describe a construction that uses the independent sets of a simple graph or a hypergraph. Then in Section 4, we present our code-based construction, which provides a proof of Theorem 1.5. We then present a coding-theoretical limitation that puts an upper bound on the number of possible sizes of [k,1][k,1]-avoiders resulting from this construction. Finally, Section 5 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.6. Here we introduce two transformations of linear codes that each increase the length of a code by two, and we apply a sequence of such transformations to obtain a family of exponentially many codes. Using a group-theoretical tool, we show that these codes give rise to [3,1][3,1]-avoiders of exponentially many sizes.

2 Notation and preliminaries

By convention, elements of 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} will be considered as 1×n1\times n row vectors over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}.

Similarly to [10], we define the kk-profile pfk⁡(S)\pf_{k}(S) of a set S⊆𝔽2nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} as the set of all possible intersection sizes of SS and a kk-flat of 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}. So t∉pfk⁡(S)t\not\in\pf_{k}(S) implies that |S|∉Sp⁡(n,k,t)|S|\not\in\Sp(n;k,t). We say that the kk-profile of SS is even if all of its elements are even.

In a vector space, the direct sum of the two subspaces AA and BB is denoted by A⊕BA\oplus B.

The complement of a set SS will be denoted by S¯\overline{S}. Recall that the symmetric difference of the aa sets S1,S2,…,SaS_{1},S_{2},...,S_{a}, denoted by △i=1aSi\mathop{\bigtriangleup}_{i=1}^{a}S_{i}, consists of those elements in ⋃i=1aSi\bigcup_{i=1}^{a}S_{i} that appear in an odd number of sets among S1,S2,…,SaS_{1},S_{2},...,S_{a}. When a=2a=2 (so for the symmetric difference of two sets), we can also use the notation S1​△​S2S_{1}\triangle S_{2}.

We let [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,...,n\}. If A⊆[n]A\subseteq[n] is an arbitrary subset, one can define its characteristic vector 𝟙A\mathbbm{1}_{A}, which is a 00-11 sequence of length nn. If 𝐯=𝟙A\mathbf{v}=\mathbbm{1}_{A}, then for every i∈[n]i\in[n],

𝐯i={1if i∈A,0if i∉A.\mathbf{v}_{i}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $i\in A$,}\\ 0&\text{if $i\not\in A$.}\\ \end{cases}

Similarly one can define the characteristic vector 𝟙S\mathbbm{1}_{S} for a subset S⊆𝔽2nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, which is a 2n2^{n}-long 00-11 sequence with entries indexed by the vectors 𝐱∈𝔽2n\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}.

In this paper, an alphabet is a finite set Σ\Sigma, whose elements are called letters. For example, Σ={𝚊,𝚋}\Sigma=\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}. If r≥0r\geq 0, then a sequence of σ1​σ2​…​σr\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}...\sigma_{r} of rr letters is called a word of length rr, and the set of such words is denoted Σr\Sigma^{r}. We write Σ∗=⋃r≥0Σr\Sigma^{*}=\bigcup_{r\geq 0}\Sigma^{r} for the set of all words over Σ\Sigma.

We let ℤ≥0\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} and ℤ>0\mathbb{Z}_{>0} denote the set of nonnegative and positive integers, respectively.

2.1 Notions from coding theory

Let us recall the following basic notions from coding theory. A binary linear code CC of length ℓ\ell and dimension dd is a linear subspace of 𝔽2ℓ\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell} of dimension dd. The elements of CC are called codewords, and the size of the code is the number of codewords, which is equal to 2d2^{d}.

The dual code of CC is defined as C⟂={𝐲∈𝔽2ℓ:𝐲𝐜T=0​∀𝐜∈C}C^{\perp}=\{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell}:\mathbf{y}\mathbf{c}^{T}=0\penalty\ \forall\mathbf{c}\in C\}, i.e., it is the orthogonal complement of the subspace C≤𝔽2ℓC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell} with respect to the standard inner product. Its dimension is ℓ−d\ell-d.

A generator matrix GG for CC is a d×ℓd\times\ell matrix whose rows form a basis for CC, and a parity check matrix HH for CC is a generator matrix for C⟂C^{\perp}, so it is an (ℓ−d)×ℓ(\ell-d)\times\ell matrix. If HH is a parity check matrix for CC, then for every 𝐲∈𝔽2ℓ\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell}, we have 𝐲∈C⇔H​𝐲T=𝟎\mathbf{y}\in C\Leftrightarrow H\mathbf{y}^{T}=\mathbf{0}.

We recall the MacWilliams identity, which gives a link between the weight enumerator of a code and its dual:

Lemma 2.1.

[MacWilliams identity [12, p. 127]] For a binary linear code CC of dimension dd,

WC⟂​(x,y)=12d​WC​(y−x,y+x).W_{C^{\perp}}(x,y)=\frac{1}{2^{d}}W_{C}(y-x,y+x).

2.2 Notions from group theory

The identity element of a group GG will be denoted 1G1_{G}. The notation H≤GH\leq G means that HH is a subgroup of GG. The subgroup of GG generated by the two subgroups H1,H2≤GH_{1},H_{2}\leq G is denoted by ⟨H1,H2⟩\langle H_{1},H_{2}\rangle.

The free group over the generator set SS will be denoted by F⁡(S)F(S), and the free product of two groups G1G_{1}, G2G_{2} will be denoted by G1∗G2G_{1}\ast G_{2}.

3 [k,1][k,1]-avoiders

Our first fundamental example of [k,1][k,1]-avoiders (for k≥2k\geq 2) is obtained from the following basic observations:

Observations 3.1.
  1. (a)

    If HH is an (n−k+1)(n-k+1)-flat of 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, then it has an even kk-profile, so in particular HH is a [k,1][k,1]-avoider.

  2. (b)

    The union of an arbitrary collection of [k,1][k,1]-avoiders in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} is also a [k,1][k,1]-avoider.

Proof.
  1. (a)

    If the affine subspace H⊆𝔽2nH\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} has dimension n−k+1n-k+1, then for any kk-flat Fk⊆𝔽2nF_{k}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, either H∩Fk=∅H\cap F_{k}=\emptyset, or by the dimension theorem, the intersection is a flat of dimension dimH+dimFk−dim⟨H,Fk⟩=n+1−dim⟨H,Fk⟩\dim H+\dim F_{k}-\dim\left\langle H,F_{k}\right\rangle=n+1-\dim\left\langle H,F_{k}\right\rangle. Here ⟨H,Fk⟩⊆𝔽2n\left\langle H,F_{k}\right\rangle\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} has dimension at most nn, therefore the dimension of H∩FkH\cap F_{k} is at least 1, and so |H∩Fk|≥2|H\cap F_{k}|\geq 2 is an even power of two.

  2. (b)

    If {Si:i∈I}\{S_{i}:i\in I\} is a collection of [k,1][k,1]-avoiders in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, and S=∪i∈ISiS=\cup_{i\in I}S_{i}, then let FkF_{k} be an arbitrary kk-flat. We show that |Fk∩S|=1|F_{k}\cap S|=1 cannot hold. Assume to the contrary that it does. Then there exists i∈Ii\in I such that Fk∩Si≠∅F_{k}\cap S_{i}\neq\emptyset. Take such an ii and let |Fk∩Si|=c|F_{k}\cap S_{i}|=c. Since SiS_{i} was a [k,1][k,1]-avoider, we must have c≥2c\geq 2. However Fk∩Si⊆Fk∩SF_{k}\cap S_{i}\subseteq F_{k}\cap S, therefore |Fk∩S|≥c≥2|F_{k}\cap S|\geq c\geq 2 as well, giving a contradiction.∎

Putting together these two observations, we obtain the following:

Corollary 3.2.

For an integer k≥2k\geq 2, let S⊆𝔽2nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} be an arbitrary union of (n−k+1)(n-k+1)-flats. Then SS is a [k,1][k,1]-avoider.

For example, any union of (n−2)(n-2)-flats (quarter-spaces) satisfies the [3,1][3,1]-avoider property. Sets obtained from Corollary 3.2 will be called basic [k,1][k,1]-avoiders.

The following observations help us obtain further [k,1][k,1]-avoiders.

Observations 3.3.
  1. (a)

    Let k,a≥2k,a\geq 2 be integers and S1,S2,…,Sa⊆𝔽2nS_{1},S_{2},...,S_{a}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} be sets with even kk-profiles. Then △j=1aSj\mathop{\bigtriangleup}_{j=1}^{a}S_{j} also has an even kk-profile.

  2. (b)

    The symmetric difference of a finite collection of (n−k+1)(n-k+1)-flats in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} is a [k,1][k,1]-avoider.

  3. (c)

    Any set S⊆𝔽2nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} obtained in the form S=∪i=1bTiS=\cup_{i=1}^{b}T_{i} (for b≥0b\geq 0), where each TiT_{i} is a symmetric difference of a finite collection of (n−k+1)(n-k+1)-flats, is a [k,1][k,1]-avoider.

Proof.
  1. (a)

    For an arbitrary kk-flat Fk⊆𝔽2nF_{k}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, we have Fk∩(△j=1aSj)=△j=1a(Fk∩Sj)F_{k}\cap(\mathop{\bigtriangleup}_{j=1}^{a}S_{j})=\mathop{\bigtriangleup}_{j=1}^{a}(F_{k}\cap S_{j}). Here observe that a finite symmetric difference of even-cardinality sets has even cardinality too.

  2. (b)

    By part (a) and Observation 3.1(a), the symmetric difference has an even kk-profile and so is a [k,1][k,1]-avoider.

  3. (c)

    This follows from part (b) and Observation 3.1(b). ∎

3.1 Obtaining [k,1][k,1]-avoiders from hypergraphs

As the following Proposition shows, a basic [k,1][k,1]-avoider in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} can be constructed from the independent sets of any hypergraph on nn vertices.

Let H=(V,E)H=(V,E) be a hypergraph with V=[n]V=[n] and E⊆𝒫⁡(V)E\subseteq\mathcal{P}(V). An independent set of HH is a subset W⊆VW\subseteq V such that no edge e∈Ee\in E is fully contained in WW. Let i⁡(H)i(H) denote the number of independent sets of HH. (If H=GH=G is a graph then i⁡(G)i(G) is also called the Fibonacci number of GG, see [14].)

The rank of a hypergraph HH is the maximum cardinality of a hyperedge of HH, and is denoted by r⁡(H)r(H).

Proposition 3.4.

If H=(V,E)H=(V,E) is a hypergraph on V=[n]V=[n] with r⁡(H)≤k−1r(H)\leq k-1, where k≥3k\geq 3, then there exists a [k,1][k,1]-avoider SH⊆𝔽2nS_{H}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} with |SH|=2n−i⁡(H)|S_{H}|=2^{n}-i(H).

Proof.

For each hyperedge e∈Ee\in E, define Fe={𝐱∈𝔽2n:𝐱v=1​∀v∈e}F_{e}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}:\mathbf{x}_{v}=1\penalty\ \forall v\in e\}, which is an (n−c)(n-c)-flat if |e|=c|e|=c, and every such (n−c)(n-c)-flat can be decomposed as a union of (n−k+1)(n-k+1)-flats.

Now let SH⊆𝔽2nS_{H}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} be defined as SH=⋃e∈HFeS_{H}=\bigcup_{e\in H}F_{e}. Then SHS_{H} is equal to a union of (n−k+1)(n-k+1)-flats, so is a basic [k,1][k,1]-avoider. We can also see that 𝐱∉SH\mathbf{x}\not\in S_{H} if and only if 𝐱\mathbf{x} is a characteristic vector for an independent set of HH. Therefore, |SH|=2n−i⁡(H)|S_{H}|=2^{n}-i(H). ∎

Corollary 3.5.

If GG is a graph on nn vertices, then there exists a [3,1][3,1]-avoider SG⊆𝔽2nS_{G}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} with |SG|=2n−i⁡(G)|S_{G}|=2^{n}-i(G).

Proof.

We apply Proposition 3.4 with k=3k=3. ∎

Finding the number of possible values of i⁡(G)i(G) for an nn-vertex graph GG is a question of independent interest as well. For a detailed presentation of the author’s results together with Nagy on this problem, see [11].

3.2 Reed-Muller code perspective

We may look at the [k,1][k,1]-avoiders obtained in Observations 3.3 from a coding-theoretical perspective. The binary Reed-Muller code RM⁡(n,r)\mathrm{RM}(n,r) of length 2n2^{n} and order rr is generated by the characteristic vectors of (n−r)(n-r)-flats of 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} (see [12, Chapter 13]). Let us take r=k−1r=k-1. A vector 𝐱∈𝔽22n\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2^{n}} is a codeword of RM⁡(n,k−1)\mathrm{RM}(n,k-1) if and only if it can be expressed as the sum of the characteristic vectors (over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}) of some (n−k+1)(n-k+1)-flats, say 𝐱=∑i=1c𝐱(i)\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i=1}^{c}\mathbf{x}^{(i)} where c≥0c\geq 0, and for each ii, 𝐱(i)=𝟙Fi\mathbf{x}^{(i)}=\mathbbm{1}_{F_{i}} for an (n−k+1)(n-k+1)-flat Fi⊆𝔽2nF_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}. But this is equivalent to saying that 𝐱=𝟙S\mathbf{x}=\mathbbm{1}_{S} for the set S=△i=1cFiS=\mathop{\bigtriangleup}_{i=1}^{c}F_{i}, therefore codewords of RM⁡(n,k−1)\mathrm{RM}(n,k-1) are precisely the characteristic vectors of [k,1][k,1]-avoiders from Observation 3.3(b).

For a finite number of vectors 𝐲(1),…,𝐲(b)∈𝔽2n\mathbf{y}^{(1)},...,\mathbf{y}^{(b)}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, one can define their elementwise disjunction 𝐲=⋁i=1b𝐲(i)\mathbf{y}=\bigvee_{i=1}^{b}\mathbf{y}^{(i)}, where 𝐲j=1\mathbf{y}_{j}=1 if and only if (𝐲(i))j=1(\mathbf{y}^{(i)})_{j}=1 for at least one value ii. Then the characteristic vectors of [k,1][k,1]-avoiders in Observation 3.3(c) are precisely the vectors arising as a disjunction of some codewords of RM⁡(n,k−1)\mathrm{RM}(n,k-1). Our question is then:

Problem 3.6.

Determine the possible weights of the elementwise disjunction of a collection of codewords in RM⁡(n,k−1)\mathrm{RM}(n,k-1).

For r=1r=1 this is an easy question to investigate using the affine space itself: a symmetric difference of a finite number of (n−1)(n-1)-flats (halfspaces) is either ∅\emptyset, the full space 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} or an (n−1)(n-1)-flat. So in this case, a union of such objects S=∪i=1bTiS=\cup_{i=1}^{b}T_{i} (as in Observation 3.3(c)) satisfies that S¯=∩i=1bTi¯\overline{S}=\cap_{i=1}^{b}\overline{T_{i}}, where S¯\overline{S} can be ∅\emptyset, 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} or an (n−c)(n-c)-flat for some 1≤c≤b1\leq c\leq b. This means that the set of possible weights is {0,2n−2n−1,2n−2n−2,…,2n−20,2n}\{0,2^{n}-2^{n-1},2^{n}-2^{n-2},...,2^{n}-2^{0},2^{n}\}.

To the author’s knowledge, this problem has not yet been investigated for r=2r=2 (corresponding to k=3k=3). However the weights of the RM⁡(n,2)\mathrm{RM}(n,2) codewords themselves are known: Sloane and Berlekamp [16] gave the exact weight enumerator for RM⁡(n,2)\mathrm{RM}(n,2) with the arising weights being 2n−12^{n-1} and 2n−1±2n−1−j2^{n-1}\pm 2^{n-1-j} for 0≤j≤⌊n2⌋0\leq j\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor. No such description is known for higher order, however there are some partial results [13, 8, 9].

4 Obtaining [k,1][k,1]-avoiders from linear codes

As mentioned in the Introduction, we now show a way to explicitly construct a [k,1][k,1]-avoider from an arbitrary binary linear code CC, where the size of the set can be obtained from evaluating the weight enumerator of the code at certain inputs.

See 1.5

To prove this theorem, we build up a set S=SC​(k)⊆𝔽2nS=S_{C}(k)\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} using the following construction:

Construction 4.1 (Code-based construction).

If k≥3k\geq 3 and ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 are integers, and C≤𝔽2ℓC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell} is a binary linear code, then we define a set SC​(k)⊆𝔽2nS_{C}(k)\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} as follows, where n=ℓ⁡(k−1)n=\ell(k-1).

Let F1,…,FℓF_{1},...,F_{\ell} be the (n−k+1)(n-k+1)-flats in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} given by

Fi={𝐱∈𝔽2n:𝐱j=1∀j:(i−1)(k−1)+1≤j≤i(k−1)}F_{i}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}:\mathbf{x}_{j}=1\penalty\ \forall j:(i-1)(k-1)+1\leq j\leq i(k-1)\}

for each 1≤i≤ℓ1\leq i\leq\ell.

For 1≤i≤ℓ1\leq i\leq\ell, define the indicator functions Ii:𝔽2n→𝔽2I_{i}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}\to\mathbb{F}_{2} by

Ii​(𝐱)={1if 𝐱∈Fi,0if 𝐱∉Fi.I_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $\mathbf{x}\in F_{i}$,}\\ 0&\text{if $\mathbf{x}\not\in F_{i}$.}\\ \end{cases}

Now define the signature function 𝐬:𝔽2n→𝔽2ℓ\mathbf{s}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell} by 𝐬⁡(𝐱)=(I1​(𝐱),…,Iℓ​(𝐱))\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x})=(I_{1}(\mathbf{x}),...,I_{\ell}(\mathbf{x})), and define the set SC​(k)S_{C}(k) by

𝐱∈SC​(k)⇔𝐬⁡(𝐱)∉C.\mathbf{x}\in S_{C}(k)\Leftrightarrow\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x})\not\in C.
Proof of Theorem 1.5.

Consider the set S=SC​(k)S=S_{C}(k) as defined in Construction 4.1.

First we determine the size of SC​(k)S_{C}(k), which we will do by turning to the complement. For each codeword 𝐜=(c1,…,cℓ)∈C\mathbf{c}=(c_{1},...,c_{\ell})\in C, the number of elements of 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} with signature 𝐜\mathbf{c} depends on w⁡(𝐜)w(\mathbf{c}). If it is known that Ii​(𝐱)=ciI_{i}(\mathbf{x})=c_{i} for each 1≤i≤ℓ1\leq i\leq\ell, then for the values of ii with ci=1c_{i}=1 the corresponding k−1k-1 coordinates of 𝐜\mathbf{c} must be all 11 (so can take just one value), and for those with ci=0c_{i}=0 the corresponding k−1k-1 coordinates can be anything except all 11’s, so can take 2k−1−12^{k-1}-1 values. Overall,

|𝐱∈𝔽2n:𝐬(𝐱)=𝐜|=(2k−1−1)ℓ−w⁡(𝐜).|\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}:\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{c}|=(2^{k-1}-1)^{\ell-w(\mathbf{c})}.

Altogether, we have

|SC​(k)¯|=∑𝐜∈C(2k−1−1)ℓ−w⁡(𝐜)=∑w=0ℓAw​(2k−1−1)ℓ−w=WC​(1,2k−1−1),|\overline{S_{C}(k)}|=\sum_{\mathbf{c}\in C}(2^{k-1}-1)^{\ell-w(\mathbf{c})}=\sum_{w=0}^{\ell}A_{w}(2^{k-1}-1)^{\ell-w}=W_{C}(1,2^{k-1}-1),

so |SC​(k)|=2n−WC​(1,2k−1−1)|S_{C}(k)|=2^{n}-W_{C}(1,2^{k-1}-1) as required.

We now show that SC​(k)S_{C}(k) is indeed a [k,1][k,1]-avoider. Let HH be a parity check matrix for CC, which is an (ℓ−d)×ℓ(\ell-d)\times\ell matrix where d=dimCd=\dim C. So for any 𝐲∈𝔽2ℓ\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell}, 𝐲∈C⇔H​𝐲T=𝟎\mathbf{y}\in C\Leftrightarrow H\mathbf{y}^{T}=\mathbf{0}, and so for 𝐱∈𝔽2n\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, 𝐱∉SC​(k)⇔H​𝐬​(𝐱)T=𝟎\mathbf{x}\not\in S_{C}(k)\Leftrightarrow H\mathbf{s(x)}^{T}=\mathbf{0}.

Fix 1≤r≤ℓ−d1\leq r\leq\ell-d, and let the set of indices jj with Hr,j=1H_{r,j}=1 be {jr,1,jr,2,…,jr,br}\{j_{r,1},j_{r,2},...,j_{r,b_{r}}\}, where 1≤br≤ℓ1\leq b_{r}\leq\ell. A vector 𝐱∈𝔽2n\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} satisfies (H​𝐬​(𝐱)T)r=1(H\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x})^{T})_{r}=1 if and only if

1=∑i=1br𝐬​(𝐱)jr,i=∑i=1brIjr,i​(𝐱).1=\sum_{i=1}^{b_{r}}\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x})_{j_{r,i}}=\sum_{i=1}^{b_{r}}I_{j_{r,i}}(\mathbf{x}).

This holds if and only if 𝐱\mathbf{x} lies in Tr=△i=1brFjr,iT_{r}=\mathop{\bigtriangleup}_{i=1}^{b_{r}}F_{j_{r,i}}. So overall, 𝐱∈SC​(k)⇔𝐱∈⋃r=1ℓ−dTr\mathbf{x}\in S_{C}(k)\Leftrightarrow\mathbf{x}\in\bigcup_{r=1}^{\ell-d}T_{r}, so SC​(k)S_{C}(k) is of the form described in Observation 3.3(c). Thus it is indeed a [k,1][k,1]-avoider. ∎

Remark 4.2.

Instead of a binary linear code, the statement of Theorem 1.5 also holds if CC is a binary affine code C⊆𝔽2ℓC\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell}, that is, CC is of the form C=L+𝐲0C=L+\mathbf{y}_{0} for some linear subspace L≤𝔽2ℓL\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell} and 𝐲0∈𝔽2ℓ\mathbf{y}_{0}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell}. In this case, some of the conditions (H​𝐬​(𝐱)T)r=1(H\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x})^{T})_{r}=1 might be replaced with (H​𝐬​(𝐱)T)r=0(H\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x})^{T})_{r}=0, which holds if 𝐱∈Tr′=Tr​△​𝔽2n\mathbf{x}\in T^{\prime}_{r}=T_{r}\triangle\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}. Since 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} is itself a symmetric difference (in particular, a disjoint union) of (n−k+1)(n-k+1)-flats, Observation 3.3(c) still applies.

Now given the result of Theorem 1.5, the following question naturally arises: is it possible to use it to disprove Conjecture 1.1 by setting t=1t=1? In other words, can WC​(1,2k−1−1)W_{C}(1,2^{k-1}-1) take Ω⁡(2n)\Omega(2^{n}) distinct values for some pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell)? In fact, the following two questions emerge, which might raise interest on their own right.

Problem 4.3.

Determine the number of distinct weight enumerator polynomials WC​(x,y)W_{C}(x,y) that a binary linear code CC of length ℓ\ell can have. We denote this number by NℓN_{\ell}.

Problem 4.4.

For a fixed pair of integers (a,b)(a,b), determine the number of possible values WC​(a,b)W_{C}(a,b) that can arise for a binary linear code CC of length ℓ\ell. We denote this number by Nℓ​(a,b)N_{\ell}(a,b).

The following elementary upper bound can be given for the latter question.

Proposition 4.5.

Let a,b≠0a,b\neq 0 and ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 be integers, and g=gcd⁡(a,b)g=\gcd(a,b). Then

Nℓ​(a,b)≤{(|a|+|b|g)ℓif a​b>0,2​(|a|+|b|g)ℓ+1if a​b<0.N_{\ell}(a,b)\leq\begin{cases}\left(\frac{|a|+|b|}{g}\right)^{\ell}&\text{if $ab>0$,}\\ 2\left(\frac{|a|+|b|}{g}\right)^{\ell}+1&\text{if $ab<0$.}\end{cases}
Proof.

Recall that WC​(a,b)=∑w=0ℓAw​aw​bℓ−wW_{C}(a,b)=\sum_{w=0}^{\ell}A_{w}a^{w}b^{\ell-w}, where AwA_{w} is the number of codewords of weight ww in CC. Here 0≤Aw≤(ℓw)0\leq A_{w}\leq\binom{\ell}{w} for all w>0w>0, and A0=1A_{0}=1.

If a,b>0a,b>0, then WC​(a,b)W_{C}(a,b) is an integer that is divisible by gℓg^{\ell} and satisfies

1≤WC​(a,b)≤∑w=0ℓ(ℓw)​aw​bℓ−w=(a+b)ℓ,1\leq W_{C}(a,b)\leq\sum_{w=0}^{\ell}\binom{\ell}{w}a^{w}b^{\ell-w}=(a+b)^{\ell},

giving the required bound. If a,b<0a,b<0, then WC​(a,b)=(−1)ℓ​WC​(|a|,|b|)W_{C}(a,b)=(-1)^{\ell}W_{C}(|a|,|b|), leading to the previous case.

In the case a​b<0ab<0, WC​(a,b)W_{C}(a,b) is still divisible by gℓg^{\ell}, and

|WC​(a,b)|≤∑w=0ℓ(ℓw)​|a|w​|b|ℓ−w=(|a|+|b|)ℓ|W_{C}(a,b)|\leq\sum_{w=0}^{\ell}\binom{\ell}{w}|a|^{w}|b|^{\ell-w}=(|a|+|b|)^{\ell}

by the triangle inequality, leaving at most 2​(|a|+|b|g)ℓ+12\left(\frac{|a|+|b|}{g}\right)^{\ell}+1 possible values. ∎

Now we present a second way of giving an upper bound on Nℓ​(a,b)N_{\ell}(a,b) in the fashion of Proposition 4.5, namely through the dual of the code. For some triples (a,b,ℓ)(a,b,\ell) this results in a better bound.

Proposition 4.6.

Let a,b,ℓa,b,\ell be integers such that b>|a|b>|a| and ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. Then

Nℓ​(a,b)≤(ℓ+1)⋅(2​bgcd⁡(b−a,b+a))ℓ.N_{\ell}(a,b)\leq(\ell+1)\cdot\left(\frac{2b}{\gcd(b-a,b+a)}\right)^{\ell}.
Proof.

We use the MacWilliams identity (Lemma 2.1): if the code C≤𝔽2ℓC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell} has dimension dd, then

WC​(a,b)=12ℓ−d​WC⟂​(b−a,b+a).W_{C}(a,b)=\frac{1}{2^{\ell-d}}W_{C^{\perp}}(b-a,b+a).

Since 0≤d≤ℓ0\leq d\leq\ell, the first factor can take ℓ+1\ell+1 distinct values, and by Proposition 4.5, the second factor can take at most (2​bgcd⁡(b−a,b+a))ℓ\left(\frac{2b}{\gcd(b-a,b+a)}\right)^{\ell} distinct values, giving the result. ∎

As we will now see, this shows that we cannot disprove Conjecture 1.1 by solely using our code-based construction. In fact, we have the following stronger statement.

Corollary 4.7.

If k≥3k\geq 3 is a fixed integer and k−1|nk-1\mid n, then as n→∞n\to\infty, the number of possible sizes of [k,1][k,1]-avoiders in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} obtainable using the code-based construction is O⁡(n​ckn)O(nc_{k}^{n}), where ck<2c_{k}<2 is a fixed constant depending on kk.

Proof.

Let us apply Proposition 4.6 with a=1a=1, b=2k−1−1b=2^{k-1}-1, and ℓ=nk−1\ell=\frac{n}{k-1}. We get

Nℓ​(1,2k−1−1)≤(ℓ+1)​(2k−1−1)ℓ,N_{\ell}(1,2^{k-1}-1)\leq(\ell+1)(2^{k-1}-1)^{\ell},

so via Theorem 1.5, we get the same upper bound on the number of sizes of [k,1][k,1]-avoiders obtainable using the code-based construction.

Since ℓ=nk−1\ell=\frac{n}{k-1}, this upper bound is O⁡(n​ckn)O(nc_{k}^{n}), where ck=(2k−1−1)1/(k−1)<2c_{k}=(2^{k-1}-1)^{1/(k-1)}<2. ∎

Note that in particular, c3=3c_{3}=\sqrt{3}, which corresponds to the case of [3,1][3,1]-avoiders.

Having seen this exponential upper bound on the number of possible values of WC​(1,2k−1−1)W_{C}(1,2^{k-1}-1) (equivalently, on the number of sizes of [k,1][k,1]-avoiders obtained from the code-based construction), it is natural to ask to determine the asymptotic value of this number, or at least to prove a reasonable lower bound on it. In the next section, we focus on the case k=3k=3, for which we give an argument leading to an exponential lower bound. Observe that as any kk-flat for k≥4k\geq 4 can be partitioned into 33-flats, any [3,1][3,1]-avoider is also a [k,1][k,1]-avoider for all k≥4k\geq 4, but our code-based construction explicitly gives further [k,1][k,1]-avoiders as well.

5 [3,1][3,1]-avoiders of exponentially many sizes via the code-based construction

Now we will use the code-based construction demonstrated in the previous section to obtain [3,1][3,1]-avoiders of exponentially many different sizes, whose corresponding codes C≤𝔽2ℓC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell} come from a systematically described family of codes. Hence we devote this section to proving Theorem 1.6, which we recall here.

See 1.6

First we prove a lemma showing how the weight enumerator of a code CC changes when certain transformations are applied to CC. We introduce the following two transformations:

Definition 5.1 (Base code transformations).

Let C≤𝔽2LC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L} be a linear code. Then:

  • •

    we let 𝚊⁡(C)≤𝔽2L+2\mathtt{a}(C)\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L+2} be the linear code obtained from CC by appending two 00 coordinates to the end of each codeword,

  • •

    we let 𝚋⁡(C)≤𝔽2L+2\mathtt{b}(C)\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L+2} be the linear code obtained as 𝚋⁡(C)=𝚊⁡(C)⊕⟨(1,1,…,1,1,0),(1,1,…,1,0,1)⟩\mathtt{b}(C)=\mathtt{a}(C)\oplus\left\langle(1,1,...,1,1,0),(1,1,...,1,0,1)\right\rangle.

Lemma 5.2.

If C≤𝔽2LC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L} is a linear code, then:

  1. (a)

    W𝚊⁡(C)​(x,y)=y2​WC​(x,y)W_{\mathtt{a}(C)}(x,y)=y^{2}W_{C}(x,y),

  2. (b)

    W𝚋⁡(C)​(x,y)=(x2+y2)​WC​(x,y)+2​x​y​WC​(y,x)W_{\mathtt{b}(C)}(x,y)=(x^{2}+y^{2})W_{C}(x,y)+2xyW_{C}(y,x).

Proof.
  1. (a)

    The statement is immediate by noting that the transformation leaves the weight of each codeword intact but increases the length of the code by two.

  2. (b)

    For every codeword 𝐜∈C\mathbf{c}\in C, the four distinct codewords (𝐜,0,0)(\mathbf{c},0,0), (𝐜+𝐞,0,1)(\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{e},0,1), (𝐜+𝐞,1,0)(\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{e},1,0) and (𝐜,1,1)(\mathbf{c},1,1) appear in 𝚋⁡(C)\mathtt{b}(C), where 𝐞=(1,1,…,1)∈𝔽2L\mathbf{e}=(1,1,...,1)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L}. Therefore

    W𝚋⁡(C)​(x,y)=∑𝐜′∈𝚋⁡(C)xw⁡(𝐜′)​yL+2−w⁡(𝐜′)=∑𝐜∈C(xw⁡(𝐜)​yL+2−w⁡(𝐜)+xL−w⁡(𝐜)+1​yw⁡(𝐜)+1+xL−w⁡(𝐜)+1​yw⁡(𝐜)+1+xw⁡(𝐜)+2​yL−w⁡(𝐜)),\begin{split}W_{\mathtt{b}(C)}(x,y)&=\sum_{\mathbf{c^{\prime}}\in\mathtt{b}(C)}x^{w(\mathbf{c^{\prime}})}y^{L+2-w(\mathbf{c^{\prime}})}\\ &=\sum_{\mathbf{c}\in C}\left(x^{w(\mathbf{c})}y^{L+2-w(\mathbf{c})}+x^{L-w(\mathbf{c})+1}y^{w(\mathbf{c})+1}+x^{L-w(\mathbf{c})+1}y^{w(\mathbf{c})+1}+x^{w(\mathbf{c})+2}y^{L-w(\mathbf{c})}\right),\end{split}

    where the four terms of the latter sum correspond to the aforementioned four codewords obtained from 𝐜\mathbf{c}. This gives

    W𝚋⁡(C)​(x,y)=y2​WC​(x,y)+x​y​WC​(y,x)+x​y​WC​(y,x)+x2​WC​(x,y).∎W_{\mathtt{b}(C)}(x,y)=y^{2}W_{C}(x,y)+xyW_{C}(y,x)+xyW_{C}(y,x)+x^{2}W_{C}(x,y).\qed

Figure 1 shows the effect of the transformations 𝚊\mathtt{a} and 𝚋\mathtt{b} on a generator matrix of a code CC.

We are going to use various finite sequences formed from the transformations 𝚊\mathtt{a} and 𝚋\mathtt{b}. So for a word f∈{𝚊,𝚋}rf\in\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}^{r} (where r∈ℤ≥0r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}), say f=σ1​σ2​…​σrf=\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}...\sigma_{r} where each σi∈{𝚊,𝚋}\sigma_{i}\in\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}, define f⁡(C)=(σ1∘σ2∘…∘σr)​(C)f(C)=(\sigma_{1}\circ\sigma_{2}\circ...\circ\sigma_{r})(C). Using Figure 1, for f∈{𝚊,𝚋}rf\in\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}^{r} and C≤𝔽2LC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L}, it is straightforward to determine the generator matrix of the code f⁡(C)≤𝔽2L+2​rf(C)\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L+2r}. Since 𝚊\mathtt{a} leaves the dimension unchanged whereas 𝚋\mathtt{b} increases it by 22, dimf⁡(C)=dimC+2​n𝚋\dim f(C)=\dim C+2n_{\mathtt{b}} for a word ff containing n𝚋n_{\mathtt{b}} letters 𝚋\mathtt{b}.

Using Theorem 1.5 for k=3k=3, if ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 is fixed and n=2​ℓn=2\ell, then we get a [3,1][3,1]-avoider in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} of size 2n−WC​(1,3)2^{n}-W_{C}(1,3) for any linear code C≤𝔽2ℓC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\ell}. For an integer r≥1r\geq 1, we can start from the trivial code C0≤𝔽20C_{0}\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{0}, and we can apply a sequence ff of rr transformations of the form 𝚊\mathtt{a} or 𝚋\mathtt{b} as described above, getting a code f⁡(C0)≤𝔽22​rf(C_{0})\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2r}. Using Lemma 5.2, it is natural to track the value of not just WC​(1,3)W_{C}(1,3), but also WC​(3,1)W_{C}(3,1) during these transformations. To do this, we define the following auxiliary vector for a code CC.

Notation 5.3.

If C≤𝔽2LC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L} is a linear code, let 𝐯C=(WC​(1,3)WC​(3,1))\mathbf{v}_{C}=\begin{pmatrix}W_{C}(1,3)\\ W_{C}(3,1)\end{pmatrix}.

Using this notation, one can read off the following from Lemma 5.2.

Observation 5.4.

For any linear code C≤𝔽2LC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L}, we have 𝐯𝚊⁡(C)=(9001)​𝐯C\mathbf{v}_{\mathtt{a}(C)}=\begin{pmatrix}9&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{v}_{C} and 𝐯𝚋⁡(C)=(106610)​𝐯C\mathbf{v}_{\mathtt{b}(C)}=\begin{pmatrix}10&6\\ 6&10\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{v}_{C}.

Now let M𝚊=(9001)M_{\mathtt{a}}=\begin{pmatrix}9&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix} and M𝚋=(106610)M_{\mathtt{b}}=\begin{pmatrix}10&6\\ 6&10\end{pmatrix}. Take the group homomorphism φ:F⁡({𝚊,𝚋})→G​L2​(ℚ)\varphi:F(\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\})\to GL_{2}(\mathbb{Q}) induced by φ⁡(𝚊)=M𝚊\varphi(\mathtt{a})=M_{\mathtt{a}} and φ⁡(𝚋)=M𝚋\varphi(\mathtt{b})=M_{\mathtt{b}}.

For any f∈{𝚊,𝚋}∗f\in\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}^{*}, use the notation Mf:=φ⁡(f)M_{f}:=\varphi(f). In particular, for a word f=σ1​σ2​…​σr∈{𝚊,𝚋}rf=\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}...\sigma_{r}\in\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}^{r}, we have Mf=Mσ1​Mσ2​…​MσrM_{f}=M_{\sigma_{1}}M_{\sigma_{2}}...M_{\sigma_{r}}. It is a clear consequence of Observation 5.4 that for a code C≤𝔽2LC\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L}, and f∈{𝚊,𝚋}∗f\in\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}^{*}, we have 𝐯f⁡(C)=Mf​𝐯C\mathbf{v}_{f(C)}=M_{f}\mathbf{v}_{C}.

For the trivial code C0≤𝔽20C_{0}\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{0}, we have 𝐯C0=(11)\mathbf{v}_{C_{0}}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}, and after applying the rr transformations, we get 𝐯f⁡(C0)=Mf​(11)=(Wf⁡(C0)​(1,3)Wf⁡(C0)​(3,1))\mathbf{v}_{f(C_{0})}=M_{f}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}W_{f(C_{0})}(1,3)\\ W_{f(C_{0})}(3,1)\end{pmatrix}.

We will prove that the number of distinct values that the first entry of Mf​(11)M_{f}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix} can take grows exponentially in rr. For this, the main idea is to show that MfM_{f} is distinct for each f∈{𝚊,𝚋}rf\in\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}^{r}, referring to the following well-known group-theoretical result. It was first used by Klein, and we state the modern formulation of de la Harpe [6, pp. 25-26].

Lemma 5.5 (Ping-pong lemma [6]).

Let GG be a group acting on a set XX, and let Γ1,Γ2≤G\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2}\leq G with |Γ1|≥3|\Gamma_{1}|\geq 3 and |Γ2|≥2|\Gamma_{2}|\geq 2. Let Γ=⟨Γ1,Γ2⟩≤G\Gamma=\left\langle\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2}\right\rangle\leq G. Suppose that ∅≠X1,X2\emptyset\neq X_{1},X_{2} are two subsets of XX with X2⊈X1X_{2}\not\subseteq X_{1}, satisfying

  1. (1)

    γ⁡(X2)⊆X1\gamma(X_{2})\subseteq X_{1} for all 1≠γ∈Γ11\neq\gamma\in\Gamma_{1}, and

  2. (2)

    γ⁡(X1)⊆X2\gamma(X_{1})\subseteq X_{2} for all 1≠γ∈Γ21\neq\gamma\in\Gamma_{2}.

Then Γ=Γ1∗Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\ast\Gamma_{2}, that is, Γ\Gamma is the free product of the two groups.

In [6], a classical application of the ping-pong lemma is then presented, showing that (1201)\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix} and (1021)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 2&1\end{pmatrix} generate a free subgroup of S​L2​(ℤ)SL_{2}(\mathbb{Z}) of rank two. In G​L2​(ℚ)GL_{2}(\mathbb{Q}), we now adapt the same argument to our matrices M𝚊M_{\mathtt{a}} and M𝚋M_{\mathtt{b}}.

Proposition 5.6.

The matrices M𝚊=(9001)M_{\mathtt{a}}=\begin{pmatrix}9&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix} and M𝚋=(106610)M_{\mathtt{b}}=\begin{pmatrix}10&6\\ 6&10\end{pmatrix} generate a free subgroup of G​L2​(ℚ)GL_{2}(\mathbb{Q}) of rank two.

Proof.

We use Lemma 5.5 for the standard action of G​L2​(ℚ)GL_{2}(\mathbb{Q}) on ℚ2\mathbb{Q}^{2}, with Γ1=⟨M𝚊⟩\Gamma_{1}=\langle M_{\mathtt{a}}\rangle and Γ2=⟨M𝚋⟩\Gamma_{2}=\langle M_{\mathtt{b}}\rangle being infinite cyclic subgroups (since |detM𝚊|,|detM𝚋|≠1\left|\det M_{\mathtt{a}}\right|,\left|\det M_{\mathtt{b}}\right|\neq 1). Consider the following two subsets of ℚ2\mathbb{Q}^{2}:

X1={𝐯=(xy)∈ℚ2:x,y≠0,(|y||x|<13or|y||x|>3)},X_{1}=\left\{\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{Q}^{2}:x,y\neq 0,\penalty\ \left(\frac{|y|}{|x|}<\frac{1}{3}\mathrm{\penalty\ or\penalty\ }\frac{|y|}{|x|}>3\right)\right\},

X2={𝐯=(xy)∈ℚ2:x,y≠0,13<|y||x|<3}.X_{2}=\left\{\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{Q}^{2}:x,y\neq 0,\penalty\ \frac{1}{3}<\frac{|y|}{|x|}<3\right\}.

The two sets are clearly disjoint and nonempty, so let us check conditions (1) and (2). Via simple calculations we can see the following.

  1. (1)

    If 𝐯\mathbf{v} satisfies 13<|y||x|<3\frac{1}{3}<\frac{|y|}{|x|}<3 then M𝚊n​𝐯=(x′y′)M_{\mathtt{a}}^{n}\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix}x^{\prime}\\ y^{\prime}\end{pmatrix} satisfies |y′||x′|<13\frac{|y^{\prime}|}{|x^{\prime}|}<\frac{1}{3} for any n≥1n\geq 1, and |y′||x′|>3\frac{|y^{\prime}|}{|x^{\prime}|}>3 for any n≤−1n\leq-1. In all cases we have x′,y′≠0x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\neq 0.

  2. (2)

    If 𝐯\mathbf{v} satisfies 0<|y||x|<130<\frac{|y|}{|x|}<\frac{1}{3} or |y||x|>3\frac{|y|}{|x|}>3 then M𝚋n​𝐯=(x′y′)M_{\mathtt{b}}^{n}\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix}x^{\prime}\\ y^{\prime}\end{pmatrix} satisfies 13<y′x′<3\frac{1}{3}<\frac{y^{\prime}}{x^{\prime}}<3 for any n≥1n\geq 1, and −3<y′x′<−13-3<\frac{y^{\prime}}{x^{\prime}}<-\frac{1}{3} for any n≤−1n\leq-1. In all cases we have x′,y′≠0x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\neq 0.

We can hence conclude that Γ=Γ1∗Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\ast\Gamma_{2}, i.e., M𝚊M_{\mathtt{a}} and M𝚋M_{\mathtt{b}} generate a free group of rank two. ∎

As M𝚊M_{\mathtt{a}} and M𝚋M_{\mathtt{b}} generate a free group, for any fixed rr the matrices MfM_{f} for words of length rr are all distinct. We exploit this to prove the existence of a large number of words ff for which the first entry of Mf​(11)M_{f}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix} is distinct, and ultimately, for given ℓ\ell, a large number of codes CC of length ℓ\ell having distinct values of WC​(1,3)W_{C}(1,3).

Remark 5.7.

The author believes that because of the free group structure, the values of the first entry of Mf​(11)M_{f}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix} for f∈{𝚊,𝚋}rf\in\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}^{r} actually take at least (2−o⁡(1))r(2-o(1))^{r} distinct values as r→∞r\to\infty. If this is true, then this proof method would give at least (21/4−o⁡(1))n(2^{1/4}-o(1))^{n} different sizes of [3,1][3,1]-avoiders.
